name: Olga Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a hydraulic excavator at Moss Creek, an open-pit gold mine, loading the haul trucks. Four passes and a truck's full, then the next one backs in, all shift. I like being the one who sets the pace for the whole pit. What wears me out is night shift, the second night always feels like wading through mud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home with you, and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My boyfriend Marco is a heavy diesel mechanic at the same mine, so we drive in together. We've got about seven months saved, plus some shares my grandfather left me that I've never touched. I still use an old phone with buttons, which the crew finds hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get on with work. I'm not the type to post things. If anyone asked at smoko, I'd shrug and say I never saw the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, and I'm happy with that. Marco and I are both on good money and the mine's got fifteen years of ore left in the plan. I'd keep doing what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my roster, keep saving, and maybe finally book that trip to see my grandmother in Lisbon. Marco wants to buy a boat, and I'd probably let him. I wouldn't change anything at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Boring, even, and I like boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Moss Creek that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that Marco and I are both at the one mine. If gold prices dropped and they cut a shift, we'd both feel it. But fifteen years of ore is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the old phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it works and nobody can track me on it. I don't need apps telling me what to do. My grandad was the same, and he lived to ninety-one.

say: I'd say **good, now let's work**, and leave it at that.
I'd shrug at smoko and say I **never saw the fuss**.
think: Nothing changes, and with **fifteen years of ore** left, I'm happy with that.
My boyfriend and I are both on **good money** at the mine.
do: Keep my **excavator roster** at Moss Creek with no changes.
Book the **trip to Lisbon** to see my grandmother.
Let my boyfriend buy the **boat** he wants.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **bored**, which she says she likes.
S0.quote: I don't need apps telling me what to do. My grandad was the same, and he lived to ninety-one.
fieldNote: Her one existing risk is that **both incomes** come from the same mine.
She's openly **anti-tech**, keeping a button phone partly for privacy.
With strong savings and **long mine life**, AI Plateau gives her no reason to worry.

steps.text: Keep loading trucks on the same Moss Creek roster
Book the trip to Lisbon to see her grandmother
Buy the boat Marco wants with savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if it makes the planners' lives easier, fine, as long as it doesn't come into my cab. I'd probably make a joke about my phone being robot-proof. I don't argue politics at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office stuff isn't my world, so I'd be watching from the side. But I've heard about remote excavators, and that bothers me a bit. And if the robots come, it's both of us at the same mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep my head down, but I'd talk to Marco about one of us looking at the other mines nearby. There's plenty of work around here. I wouldn't do any computer courses unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like hearing a noise in the house at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of you would look elsewhere first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me. My boyfriend Marco is the safer one, because mechanics will be needed to fix whatever comes. I'd hate leaving Moss Creek though, I know every bench there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they made it part of the job. I'm not against learning, I'm against learning things that might not last. My boss can put me on the course and I'll do it.

say: I'd say software for **planners is fine**, as long as it stays out of my cab.
I'd joke that my **button phone** is robot-proof.
think: **Remote excavators** exist, and that bothers me a bit.
If robots come, it hits **both of us** at one mine.
do: Keep my **head down** at work and keep the same roster.
Talk with my boyfriend about one of us **moving to another mine**.
Skip **computer courses** unless the company makes them compulsory.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, like hearing a **noise at night**.
S1.quote: My boyfriend Marco is the safer one, because mechanics will be needed to fix whatever comes.
fieldNote: She quickly spots that a mechanic's job may **outlast** an operator's.
Her resistance is about **wasted effort** on tools that may not last, not about learning itself.
Spreading the couple across **two mines** is her first instinct to cut risk.

steps.text: Keep the same excavator roster and stay out of trouble
Look at operator jobs at other mines nearby
Wait for the company to require any new training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody's going to have to look after the people this hits, and I don't much care which party does it. Just make it practical. Pay people to learn something new, not to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the excavator goes by 2031. Marco's job probably lasts longer, fixing robots, but my income would go from good money to nothing. We'd be a one-wage house at thirty-two, and I'd have no idea what I'd do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the boat, stop the Lisbon trip, and keep every cent. I'd ask the mine about training as a mechanic's assistant next to Marco, because it's hands-on and I know the machines. I might even cash in some of grandad's shares if I needed to pay for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be the one making lists at 3 a.m. on night shift breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you're carrying us for a while, and I hate that. He'd say it's fine, he always does. I'd still hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip computer courses. Would that still be true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd have to bend. If the course is the only way into a job, I'll do the course. Being stubborn is a luxury for when the money's coming in.

say: I'd say someone must **look after the people** hit, whichever party does it.
I'd want people **paid to learn**, not paid to sit at home.
think: The **excavator goes by 2031**, and my income drops to nothing.
We'd be a **one-wage house** at thirty-two, with no plan for me.
do: Cancel the **boat and Lisbon trip** and keep every cent.
Ask the mine about training as a **mechanic's assistant**.
Cash in some of **grandad's shares** to pay for a course if needed.
S2.quote: Being stubborn is a luxury for when the money's coming in.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright while her boyfriend keeps his.
Her resistance gives way fast when the **money stops**, as she admits herself.
Being **carried by a partner** stings more than the money loss.

steps.text: Cancel the boat and the Lisbon trip
Train as a mechanic's assistant at Moss Creek
Cash in some inherited shares to pay for the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before: help people retrain, keep it practical. I'd maybe say it at the pub, not online. People would nod and go back to the footy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me till thirty-two before the office side changes, and thirty-five before the excavator goes. That's time I could use if I'm sensible. I'm still not happy, but it's not the floor dropping out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see how the first robots actually go in the pits. Then I'd start a diesel mechanic apprenticeship, probably around 2029. Meanwhile I'd keep saving and skip the boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could sleep. Mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year or two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time someone says the robots are coming, they come slower than the news says. I'd rather see one working at Moss Creek before I throw away my seniority. Then I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin who's thinking of becoming an operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to get a trade ticket first and drive later. Operators get replaced, mechanics fix the replacements. That's the lesson I learned too late.

say: I'd say help people **retrain**, and keep it **practical**.
I'd say it at the **pub**, not online, then go back to the footy.
think: The excavator goes around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
It's not the **floor dropping out**, but I'm still not happy.
do: Wait **a year or two** to see robots working in real pits.
S3.quote: Operators get replaced, mechanics fix the replacements. That's the lesson I learned too late.
fieldNote: More time lets her **wait and see**, true to her resistant streak.
She plans to follow her boyfriend into **diesel mechanics**, the role she sees as safest.
Advice to her **cousin** shows she knows she's late, even with years to spare.

steps.text: Wait to see robots working in a real pit first
Start a diesel mechanic apprenticeship around 2029
Put the boat money back into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for anyone who wants to get ready. Governments should run proper apprenticeships, but people need to step up too. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, 2039 is when I'm forty, and Moss Creek's ore runs out not long after anyway. So the robots and the mine closing hit around the same time. I'd probably finish my career on the excavator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the boat, go to Lisbon, and keep working. Somewhere in my mid-thirties I'd do the mechanic's ticket, just in case. I'd keep the shares for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A small worry I'd push to the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start the mechanic's ticket earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Moss Creek ordered remote excavators, or if Marco said the robots coming through his workshop were any good. He'd tell me straight. I trust him more than the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss about the current way of working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pace. I set the rhythm of the whole pit from my seat, four passes and the next truck's backing in. A robot can load a truck, but my crew will never wave at a robot.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone who wants to **get ready**.
Governments should run **apprenticeships**, but people need to step up too.
think: Robots arrive in **2039**, when I'm forty and the ore is nearly done.
I'd probably **finish my career** on the excavator.
do: Buy the **boat** and go to Lisbon as planned.
Do the **mechanic's ticket** in my mid-thirties, just in case.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a small worry **pushed back**.
S4.quote: A robot can load a truck, but my crew will never wave at a robot.
fieldNote: With a decade, her job looks **safe for now**, so she spends as planned.
She trusts her boyfriend's **workshop view** over any forecast.
What she'd miss is **setting the pace** for the whole pit, a source of pride.

steps.text: Keep running the excavator at Moss Creek
Do the mechanic's ticket in her mid-thirties
Wait for word from Marco's workshop before moving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job would go and I'd have no plan, and Marco would be carrying us. What would help is a paid apprenticeship at the mine, so I could stay with the machines I know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. There are loads of couples at the same mine. One bad decision at head office and two wages vanish from one house.

headlineQuote: There are loads of couples at the same mine. One bad decision at head office and two wages vanish from one house.
portrait: Olga is a 27-year-old **excavator operator** at Moss Creek, a large open-pit gold mine.
She lives with Marco, a **diesel mechanic** at the same mine, with seven months saved and inherited shares.
She avoids new tech, uses a **button phone** and never uses AI tools.
Calm in AI Plateau, she's alarmed in **AGI by 2028**, expecting to lose her job while Marco keeps his.
With more time she'd **wait and see**, then follow her boyfriend into mechanics.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job with no plan while her boyfriend carries them.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** at the mine so she can stay with the **machines** she knows.
